# `ocr-layer.pdf` — provenance, and the measured facts the overlay is built against

**Generated by `tools/gen-ocr-layer-fixture.py`.** That script carries the full
argument for the document's shape; this file carries the *numbers*, and every
one of them is read out of the engine rather than computed by hand. Regenerate
with:

    python tools/gen-ocr-layer-fixture.py

Deterministic — same bytes every time, no timestamps, no object ids. 1,799
bytes, MD5 `dbe0d592bedd76513bd5cf744b388ac5`. One page, `/MediaBox [0 0 612
792]`, nine objects, three uncompressed content streams, a classic
cross-reference table, base-14 Helvetica twice.

## What it is, in one line

A page that already carries an OCR text layer — text shown at rendering mode 3,
invisible, over a picture — readable **without the recogniser and without the
model weights**.

## Why it is not `synthetic-image-only.pdf`

That fixture is the opposite case and the right one for its own job: a page
with *no* text, built so the recogniser has something to recognise. Producing
an OCR'd document from it costs the ~12 MB `ocrs` weights, which are not in
this repository, several seconds of CPU, and a result that changes whenever the
model does. `crates/pdfcer-gui/src/ocr/fixture.rs` owns that half and its header
is explicit that a green result there establishes the plumbing and nothing
about recognition quality.

This file is the half downstream of the recogniser: the sandwich as the engine
writes it, frozen, cheap, and byte-identical on every machine.

## What it is NOT

**It is not a scan.** Its picture is an eight-by-eight checkerboard, not an
image of the words the invisible layer spells. Nothing here measures
recognition quality, glyph placement accuracy, or whether an OCR layer lines up
with the ink beneath it. A check that wants those needs a real scan, and this
project does not have one.

## The three content streams

Object 4 is the picture and the visible stamp; object 6 is the OCR layer;
object 9 is the rendering-mode ladder. `/Contents [4 0 R 6 0 R 9 0 R]`, in that
order.

Object 6 copies `pdfcer_core::ocr::layer::build_layer_content`'s emission shape
exactly — `q` `BT` `3 Tr`, then one `Tf`/`Tz`/`Tm`/`Tj` group per word, then
`ET` `Q` — and the font it names is `/pdfceF1`, which is what
`text_edit::addtext::pick_font_name` yields on a page whose `/Font` has no such
key. The `q`/`Q` wrapper is load-bearing: `Tf`, `Tr` and `Tz` are graphics
state and must not leak into the stream that follows.

## The three controls, and the wrong build each one catches

| control | where | a build that fails it |
|---|---|---|
| a visible run on the same page | `VISIBLE CONTROL STAMP`, object 4 | reports every glyph invisible |
| a hidden run outside the OCR stream | ladder, first run | decides invisibility by content stream |
| a visible run after a hidden one, same `BT`…`ET` | ladder, second run | treats mode 3 as latching to `ET` |

The second and third are the ones the overlay turns on. A shell that
reimplements the mode judgement from the content stream — rather than reading
the flag `pdfcer_core::text_extract::ExtractedGlyph::invisible` already carries
— gets the ladder wrong, and the ladder is the only place on this page where
getting it wrong is visible.

## What is deliberately absent

A stream that sets `3 Tr` and never restores it, leaving everything after it
invisible. Real producers ship that defect, and it is a torture case for the
*extractor*, not for the overlay: on such a page the correct answer is "all of
it is invisible", which is also the answer a broken build gives. It belongs in
its own fixture with its own argument.

## The glyph counts

| | glyphs |
|---|---|
| OCR layer (nine words) | 44 |
| ladder, hidden run | 30 |
| **invisible, total** | **74** |
| stamp | 21 |
| ladder, visible run | 30 |
| **visible, total** | **51** |
| all | 125 |

`TextDiagnostics::invisible_glyphs` reports **74** on its own tally path, which
is the same claim reached a second way. Both are asserted; a change that moved
one and not the other is a finding about the engine rather than about this
fixture.

## The twenty-one runs

The extractor splits the page into 21 runs, nine of which are whitespace
joiners with no glyphs. Two facts about that shape a check may trip over:

* **There is no run whose text is `SHEET`.** `SHEET` at x = 225 and `2` at
  x = 272 fall inside the word-space threshold at 14 pt, so they arrive merged
  as `SHEET2`, six glyphs.
* **`SCANNED` appears twice**, at baselines y = 676 and y = 652, and both runs
  have exactly that text. Code that looks it up by string must expect two.

## The horizontal-scale control

The engine emits a per-word `Tz` so an OCR word's glyphs span the box the
recogniser found. A reader that drops `Tz` gets every OCR run's extent wrong
without getting anything visibly wrong — the page still looks right, because
none of this text is drawn.

The control has to be the **same word at two scales**: comparing two different
words confounds the scale with the letters, since `I` is narrow and `W` is not.
So `SCANNED` is written twice, identical in text and size, `Tz 100` on the
upper baseline and `Tz 86.4` on the lower.

| | span, summed glyph advances |
|---|---|
| `SCANNED` at `Tz 100` | 68.44601 pt |
| `SCANNED` at `Tz 86.4` | that × 0.864, measured to within 0.001 |

## The raster, and the property the whole overlay rests on

**The OCR layer reaches no pixel.** The operator sees the invisible layer only
because the shell draws it, never because the rasterizer does. If mode-3 text
reached the pixmap, the overlay would be a second rendering of content the page
already shows, the transparency slider would be compositing a picture with
itself, and R8b's *applied content renders exactly as saved content will
render* would be false of every OCR'd page.

Measured by rendering twice at scale 2.0 and comparing every pixel: once as
saved, once against a control built from the fixture's own bytes with
`/Contents` rewritten to `[4 0 R 9 0 R]`, space-padded to the same width so no
offset moves and the cross-reference table stays correct. The two rasters are
identical.

The control is guarded from the other side too, because a build that rasterized
a blank page would satisfy "identical". The as-saved raster carries **490,039**
dark pixels, against a floor of 1,000 asserted in the test — the checkerboard
alone is a quarter of the sheet in solid black. Making the layer visible as a
plant moves that to 493,467, so the layer's own contribution when it is allowed
to draw is 3,428 pixels: small, which is exactly why a pixel comparison and not
an eyeball is the instrument.

## The picture

Eight by eight, `/DeviceGray`, eight bits, uncompressed, sixty-four bytes,
scaled to the full sheet so each cell is 76.5 × 99 points.

Pure black and pure white, not two greys, because the slider this fixture
exists to serve has to be decidable from a screenshot at three positions: at
0.0 the raster is drawn as saved, at 0.5 it is tinted, and at 1.0 it is not
drawn at all. Two mid-greys make *tinted* and *blanked* look alike.

The top half is the checkerboard and the bottom half is flat white, so the
invisible OCR words sit high on the page over the pattern, where scanned words
would be, and the visible controls sit low over white, where they stay legible
in a screenshot.

## Who depends on this file

* `crates/pdfcer-gui/src/ocr/layer_fixture.rs` — owns every number above and
  fails with the live figure quoted when one moves. Its `dump_the_ocr_layer_fixture`
  is `#[ignore]`d and prints the run table, so the constants can be re-derived
  rather than trusted.
